university: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Policy (AI-001)
documents.stance_why: The policy is an institution-wide AI governance policy: it "fosters innovation", "encourages education and research in AI", and allows AI use under conditions (verification, approved tools, assessment, training). It sets no rule for student coursework, so permit with conditions fits better than delegates.
documents.summary: Effective 2025-12-01 governance policy for developing, buying and using AI at UTRGV. It covers roles (AI Risk Officer, Governance Committee), ethical use, data protection, risk assessment, procurement and training; it says almost nothing about student coursework or academic integrity beyond verification and accountability.

units.why: The purpose statement sets the institution-wide framing: it "fosters innovation while protecting privacy, fairness, security, and academic integrity". It is a preamble of purpose, so P56; it binds no one specifically (all) and is a principle (informs).
units.anchor: UTRGV fosters innovation while protecting privacy, fairness, security, and academic integrity

units.why: Scope clause defining who the policy covers ("faculty, staff, students, contractors, and vendors") and which activity (design, procurement, configuration, deployment of AI systems). Scope definition goes under P61; it is general/informs.
units.anchor: applies to faculty, staff, students, contractors, and vendors who design, procure, configure, or deploy AI
units.fit_note: The scope is people who design, procure, configure or deploy AI systems, not students who merely use AI tools in coursework.

units.why: A definition of AI ("simulation of human intelligence processes by machines") that fixes what the policy covers, so P61, phase general, modality informs.
units.anchor: Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines

units.why: Defines Generative AI ("can create new content, such as text, images, or music"), setting the policy's vocabulary; P61, informs.
units.anchor: A type of AI that can create new content, such as text, images, or music

units.why: Names the officer and committee that run the AI policy ("AI Risk Officer (AIRO)" and "AI Governance Committee"). Naming who owns the policy is P80; it is institutional set-up (before-course) addressed to the university (admin).
units.anchor: designates AI Risk Officer (AIRO) and establishes an AI Governance Committee

units.why: States the committee's duties: it "sets standards, reviews heightened-risk deployments, approves assessment instruments". Who interprets and enforces the policy is P80.
units.anchor: The AI Governance Committee sets standards, reviews heightened‑risk deployments

units.why: The AIRO "ensures that an AI Inventory is established and maintained" and "coordinates assessments and monitoring". Documenting and monitoring deployed AI systems is P98; it continues over time.
units.anchor: ensures that an AI Inventory is established and maintained
units.policy: The AIRO ensures that an AI Inventory is established and maintained, classifies risk, coordinates assessments and monitoring, and reports on incidents and program maturity.

units.why: The committee "ensures mandatory training is provided", i.e. the institution mandates AI training, which is P70. The training is not tied to courses so phase is before-course set-up.
units.anchor: ensures mandatory training is provided

units.why: Binds units (admin) to "ethical and compliant use of AI" in their operations; a duty to comply with law and policy, so P77.
units.anchor: Units remain responsible for the ethical and compliant use of AI within their operations

units.why: Users are "responsible for abiding by all established laws, rules, regulations, policies" on ethical AI use, which is the compliance rule P77.
units.anchor: Users are responsible for abiding by all established laws, rules, regulations, policies

units.why: Bans "discriminatory, biased, malicious, or harmful use of AI" for all users. A general conduct ban on malicious AI use is P74.
units.anchor: Discriminatory, biased, malicious, or harmful use of AI is strictly prohibited

units.why: "All AI development projects, applications or the use of AI driven automated decision making must undergo an ethical review by the data owner" is a required review before use; closest is P65 (institutional review of AI systems).
units.anchor: must undergo an ethical review by the data owner
units.policy: All AI development projects, applications or the use of AI driven automated decision making must undergo an ethical review by the data owner.
units.fit_note: The review is an ethical impact review by the data owner, not a security, legal or procurement review.

units.why: Users "must respect the privacy rights of individuals and handle personal, sensitive, and confidential data" lawfully; data protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: handle personal, sensitive, and confidential data in accordance with relevant laws

units.why: Users must follow IP and copyright law, and "unauthorized distribution, copying, or modification of AI-related resources is prohibited". This is an IP rule, so P52.
units.anchor: Unauthorized distribution, copying, or modification of AI-related resources is prohibited
units.fit_note: Concerns IP in AI software, models and datasets, not ownership of AI output.

units.why: Requires "clear user/public notices where applicable" and not misrepresenting "AI as human", i.e. telling people when they deal with AI (P103).
units.anchor: do not misrepresent AI as human
units.policy: Provide clear user/public notices where applicable and do not misrepresent AI as human.

units.why: Requires labeling "synthetic media" and provenance measures (watermarking, metadata) for generative outputs. P103 is about people knowing they interact with AI; labeling generated content is a different rule, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Label synthetic media and use content provenance measures
units.uncovered_note: Generated media must be labeled and carry provenance metadata where feasible.

units.why: "Maintain system/model cards" is documentation of deployed AI systems, which P98 names (model cards, records).
units.anchor: Maintain system/model cards for applicable public‑facing systems

units.why: Requires "complaint and redress channels" about AI outcomes. Closest is P71 (a channel to report AI problems).
units.anchor: Offer complaint and redress channels with published response expectations
units.fit_note: Channel is for people affected by AI system outcomes to complain and seek redress, with published response times.

units.why: Users "must take measures to ensure the security of AI systems, including protecting access to credentials" and applying patches. No type covers general security duties for AI systems (P75 is phishing awareness), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Users must take measures to ensure the security of AI systems
units.uncovered_note: General security hygiene for AI systems: protect credentials, patch, follow ISO requirements.

units.why: Requires AI models be "designed and tested to minimize bias and discrimination", naming bias as a concern (P53); it speaks to developers more than to course use.
units.anchor: AI algorithms and models must be designed and tested to minimize bias and discrimination
units.fit_note: States a design and testing duty rather than only naming the concern.

units.why: Involving "students, faculty, staff, administrators, regulators" is "encouraged" where appropriate, a form of community engagement on AI; nearest type P88.
units.anchor: the participation of students, faculty, staff, administrators, regulators
units.policy: Where appropriate, the participation of students, faculty, staff, administrators, regulators, and or others deemed appropriate external parties that may be affected is encouraged.
units.fit_note: Stakeholders are involved in AI projects affecting them; P88 is about peers, partners and public forums.

units.why: States that "UTRGV encourages education and research in AI and related fields", an institution-level welcome of AI work. P02 covers encouragement of AI; it does not set student coursework rules.
units.anchor: UTRGV encourages education and research in AI and related fields
units.fit_note: Encourages AI education and research as a field, not student use of AI tools in courses.

units.why: "Regularly assess and mitigate bias" plus "continuous monitoring and testing" is ongoing monitoring of AI for bias, which P98 covers.
units.anchor: Regularly assess and mitigate bias to ensure equitable outcomes
units.policy: Users should strive to eliminate bias from AI systems and promote fairness in their applications. Regularly assess and mitigate bias to ensure equitable outcomes.

units.why: Users are "responsible for ensuring that any AI-generated content they choose to use has been independently verified", the verify-AI-output rule (P31).
units.anchor: any AI-generated content they choose to use has been independently verified for accuracy and reliability

units.why: "Individuals using AI technologies are accountable for their actions and decisions facilitated by AI systems": users own the outcomes, P29.
units.anchor: Individuals using AI technologies are accountable for their actions and decisions
units.fit_note: Applies to all individuals using AI, not specifically to submitted student work.

units.why: "Do not solely rely on AI recommendations when making important choices" keeps humans responsible for consequential decisions, P73.
units.anchor: Do not solely rely on AI recommendations when making important choices
units.fit_note: Applies to important choices generally, not only decisions about people.

units.why: Data must be collected per UTRGV and UT System guidance with notices or consents, and users are told to contact the "Information Security Office" for acceptable use of data in AI. Data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: Contact the Information Security Office for further guidance related to the acceptable use
units.policy: Data used in AI applications must be collected in accordance with existing UTRGV and UT System guidance and all applicable laws including appropriate notices or consents.

units.why: Says AI systems "should be designed to be accessible to all, including individuals with disabilities", which is accessibility of AI (P97).
units.anchor: should be designed to be accessible to all, including individuals with disabilities

units.why: The Prohibited Activities section only says users "must refrain from engaging in any conduct that violates" university, system, state or federal policy or law, a compliance rule (P77).
units.anchor: Users must refrain from engaging in any conduct that violates UTRGV, UT System

units.why: "Controlled and confidential data may only be used with approved AI tools that have been evaluated by IT and the Information Security Office": protect sensitive data by using vetted tools, P50 (not P92, which is about using licensed tools generally).
units.anchor: may only be used with approved AI tools that have been evaluated by IT

units.why: Even for public data, "all AI tools must undergo and pass the necessary IT and ISO technology assessment processes", an institutional tool-approval rule, P65.
units.anchor: all AI tools must undergo and pass the necessary IT and ISO technology assessment processes

units.why: Requires an AI Risk Assessment (security, limitations, foreseeable harm, accuracy, uptime) "before deployment and after material changes"; review before deployment is P65.
units.anchor: complete an AI Risk Assessment
units.policy: Before deployment and after material changes, complete an AI Risk Assessment (security risks, limitations, foreseeable harm(s), and operational metrics: accuracy, latency, uptime, error rate).

units.why: The AI Impact Assessment covers stakeholders, training data, "ownership of monitoring and cadence" and retention; it documents and sets up monitoring of AI systems (P98).
units.anchor: Complete an AI Impact Assessment addressing stakeholders, training data description

units.why: A "Human Oversight Plan for consequential uses" with "authority to stop/override" keeps humans in charge of consequential AI use; nearest is P73.
units.anchor: Provide a Human Oversight Plan for consequential uses
units.policy: Provide a Human Oversight Plan for consequential uses (reviewer qualifications, QA sampling, escalation thresholds, authority to stop/override).
units.fit_note: Applies to consequential AI uses generally, not only decisions about individuals.

units.why: Deployment of heightened-risk AI needs "approval from the AI Governance Committee and AIRO sign-off", an approval step before deployment (P65).
units.anchor: Obtain approval from the AI Governance Committee and AIRO sign‑off prior to deployment

units.why: "AI use at UTRGV must comply with relevant Federal laws, State of Texas regulations, UT System policies, and UTRGV rules": a compliance duty, P77.
units.anchor: AI use at UTRGV must comply with relevant Federal laws, State of Texas regulations

units.why: Separate rule that AI systems "must comply with GDPR requirements"; it is a legal compliance rule, P77.
units.anchor: AI systems must comply with GDPR requirements regarding data protection and privacy

units.why: "All non-student UTRGV account holders ... must complete AI training provided by the Information Security Office annually" is mandated AI training for staff, P70.
units.anchor: must complete AI training provided by the Information Security Office annually
units.policy: All non-student UTRGV account holders with access to UTRGV resources must complete AI training provided by the Information Security Office annually.

units.why: Systems offering AI "must undergo a Technology Assessment ... before purchase (including open-source or free products)", review of AI tools before purchase, P65.
units.anchor: must undergo a Technology Assessment through UTRGV approved workflows before purchase

units.why: AI development "must comply with all approval and change management procedures"; an approval requirement for building AI, nearest P65.
units.anchor: The development of AI solutions must comply with all approval and change management procedures
units.fit_note: Covers approval and change management for AI development, not only tool purchase.

units.why: Procurement "contracts must require alignment with NIST AI RMF, transparency documentation (system/model cards)", institutional review of AI vendors and contracts, P65.
units.anchor: Contracts must require alignment with NIST AI RMF, transparency documentation
units.policy: Contracts must require alignment with NIST AI RMF, transparency documentation (system/model cards), material change notifications, security posture, and audit rights.

units.why: Requires "periodic reassessment for heightened-risk vendor systems", the periodic re-evaluation included in P65.
units.anchor: Ensure periodic reassessment for heightened‑risk vendor systems

units.why: "Non-compliance may result in suspension of system access or use and other actions" states consequences for breaking the policy; closest is P37, though not a specific penalty schedule.
units.anchor: Non‑compliance may result in suspension of system access or use
units.fit_note: The consequence is a general sanction (suspension of access) for the whole policy, not a penalty for student AI misuse.

units.why: "This policy will be reviewed at least annually or upon significant regulatory or technological change" is a review cycle, P54.
units.anchor: This policy will be reviewed at least annually

documents.unit: Center for Online Learning and Teaching Technology (COLTT)
documents.title: Generative AI Technology
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to "clearly outline expectations" and decide "whether AI use is permitted or restricted" in their syllabus, and sets no university rule on student use, so it delegates to instructors.
documents.summary: Faculty-facing resource from the online-teaching center on what generative AI is, how to set syllabus expectations, how to redesign assessments, and cautions on AI detectors. It leaves the decision to each instructor.

units.why: "A critical first step is becoming familiar with Generative AI tools ... try using these tools yourself" advises instructors to learn the tools before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: try using these tools yourself
units.policy: A critical first step is becoming familiar with Generative AI tools, their capabilities, and their limitations. In addition to reading about them, try using these tools yourself.

units.why: Defines generative AI as systems "designed to create new content" (text, images, code, audio), P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI refers to a category of Artificial Intelligence systems designed to create new content

units.why: The page warns models can produce "factually incorrect, incomplete, or biased outputs" so "it is important to verify", P31.
units.anchor: it is important to verify AI-generated information before using it in academic or professional work

units.why: Lists "Completing programming assignments" among concerns about misuse. It names a misuse without ruling on it, so informs; nearest type is P19 (AI producing submitted work).
units.anchor: Completing programming assignments
units.fit_note: Names misuse concerns (essays, exam answers, programming, math) but does not itself prohibit them.

units.why: Tells instructors to "clearly outline expectations" in the syllabus: whether AI is permitted or restricted, citation, and consequences. That is P09.
units.anchor: Clearly outline expectations regarding the use of Generative AI tools in your course
units.policy: Clearly outline expectations regarding the use of Generative AI tools in your course. This may include: Whether AI use is permitted or restricted Expectations for citation or acknowledgment Consequences for inappropriate use

units.why: "Policies should align with course learning outcomes and institutional guidance" ties AI decisions to learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: Policies should align with course learning outcomes and institutional guidance

units.why: "Equally important is having open conversations with students about Generative AI" including capabilities, limits and ethics, so instructors explain and discuss rules (P66).
units.anchor: having open conversations with students about Generative AI
units.policy: Equally important is having open conversations with students about Generative AI.

units.why: Instructors are told to "encourage transparency by asking students to acknowledge AI use when appropriate", a soft disclosure expectation, P24.
units.anchor: Encourage transparency by asking students to acknowledge AI use when appropriate
units.fit_note: Disclosure is encouraged and conditional ("when appropriate"), not required.

units.why: "Too much reliance on AI shortcuts can limit opportunities to develop essential skills" gives the skill-building reason for limiting AI, P41.
units.anchor: Too much reliance on AI shortcuts can limit opportunities to develop essential skills

units.why: "Lower-stakes assessments can reduce pressure and discourage misuse" so instructors "consider avoiding high-stakes weighting". It eases the pressure behind misuse, P99 not P33.
units.anchor: consider avoiding high-stakes weighting
units.policy: If exams or quizzes are used, consider avoiding high-stakes weighting. Lower-stakes assessments can reduce pressure and discourage misuse while supporting skill development.

units.why: Suggests per-question time limits (e.g. "60 seconds per multiple-choice question") so students cannot search externally; a redesign of assessment format, P35.
units.anchor: Appropriate time limits can reduce opportunities to search for answers externally
units.policy: Consider Time Limits: Appropriate time limits can reduce opportunities to search for answers externally.

units.why: Suggests "Lockdown browsers with monitoring" to deter misconduct, a closed-device exam measure, so P22.
units.anchor: Lockdown browsers with monitoring features may help deter misconduct
units.fit_note: Offered as an optional deterrent for online exams, not as a ban on AI in exams.

units.why: AI detection tools "are not definitive and should never be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions": detector output is supporting evidence only, P69 (not P39, since detectors may still be used).
units.anchor: they are not definitive
units.policy: AI detection tools may help identify content potentially generated by AI, but they are not definitive and should never be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions.

units.why: Tells instructors to "use a plagiarism detection tool such as Turnitin to support academic integrity", a similarity check, P40.
units.anchor: Use a plagiarism detection tool such as
units.policy: Use a plagiarism detection tool such as Turnitin to support academic integrity.

units.why: Instructors should "review originality reports carefully" because similarity percentages "do not automatically indicate plagiarism", an evidence standard, P69.
units.anchor: similarity percentages may include properly cited sources and reference lists
units.policy: It is important to review originality reports carefully, as similarity percentages may include properly cited sources and reference lists and do not automatically indicate plagiarism.

units.why: Turnitin's AI writing results "are not always accurate and should not be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions", an unreliability warning about detectors, P39.
units.anchor: these results are not always accurate
units.policy: Turnitin also offers an AI writing assessment to help identify text that may be AI-generated; however, these results are not always accurate and should not be used as the sole basis for academic misconduct decisions.

units.why: "Human judgment and institutional academic policies must guide any final determinations" keeps a human as the decider on misconduct, P73.
units.anchor: Human judgment and institutional academic policies must guide any final
units.fit_note: Applies to misconduct determinations that rest on detector output.

units.why: "Using clear rubrics with well-defined criteria can help deter inappropriate AI use" changes grading design in response to AI, P35.
units.anchor: Using clear
units.policy: Using clear rubrics with well-defined criteria can help deter inappropriate AI use by clarifying expectations and emphasizing original thinking and analysis.

units.why: Instructors should "design assignments that require students to connect course content to personal experiences, current events, or reflective analysis" because AI struggles to replicate these; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Design assignments that require students to connect course content to

units.why: Gives the career reason for teaching with AI: "students are likely to encounter AI tools in the workplace", P44.
units.anchor: Since students are likely to encounter AI tools in the workplace

units.why: Instructors "may consider designing activities that intentionally incorporate AI use" focused on "evaluation, reflection, critique, and ethical application"; AI built into coursework, P79.
units.anchor: intentionally incorporate AI use
units.policy: Instructors may consider designing activities that intentionally incorporate AI use, focusing on evaluation, reflection, critique, and ethical application rather than avoidance alone.
units.fit_note: Optional suggestion to build AI into activities, not a requirement.

units.why: Lists "providing formative feedback on writing" among ways AI "can support education"; it is a permitted use for writing support, nearest P91.
units.anchor: Providing formative feedback on writing
units.fit_note: Describes AI giving feedback on writing, not editing the student's text.

units.why: Names "generating summaries, flashcards, or practice questions" as a use of AI in education, a study-aid use, P14.
units.anchor: Generating summaries, flashcards, or practice questions

units.why: "Assisting with tutoring and step-by-step explanations" is an AI-as-tutor use, P12.
units.anchor: Assisting with tutoring and step-by-step explanations

units.why: Listed as a use: "helping create instructional materials or assessments", instructor use of AI for teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: Helping create instructional materials or assessments

units.why: Names "supporting accessibility through alternative formats and summaries" as a use, AI as an accessibility aid, P97.
units.anchor: Supporting accessibility through alternative formats and summaries

units.why: "Generative AI should not replace instructors, but rather assist educators", limiting instructor-side AI use to assisting; P59.
units.anchor: Generative AI should not replace instructors
units.policy: Generative AI should not replace instructors, but rather assist educators in supporting learning, providing feedback, and enhancing engagement when used thoughtfully and responsibly.
units.fit_note: Sets a limit that AI assists and does not replace instructors, rather than listing allowed tasks.

units.why: The page "will continue to be updated with new guidance, resources, and recommended readings", a statement that guidance is provisional, P54.
units.anchor: will continue to be updated with new guidance, resources, and recommended readings

documents.title: Learner-Centered Syllabus Design (generative AI syllabus statements)
documents.stance_why: The center offers three suggested optional statements (exploratory, permitted as specified, no use) that instructors may "modify as you see fit", so the choice is handed to instructors and tiers are listed.
tiers: Permitted use as specified by the instructor
documents.summary: Syllabus design page whose AI section gives three optional sample statements that range from embedding AI to banning it entirely. Instructors choose and adapt; the page sets no university default.

units.why: Asks each instructor to "consider how you want to approach generative AI technologies in your courses" and to "modify as you see fit": the center sets no rule, instructors decide, P04.
units.anchor: please consider how you want to approach generative AI technologies in your courses

units.why: Says the sample statements "are only an example and optional" for syllabi, leaving the choice to instructors, P04.
units.anchor: These potential approaches are only an example and optional
units.policy: Please modify as you see fit and align to your teaching values, beliefs, and course learning objectives. These potential approaches are only an example and optional in case you would like to include in your syllabus.

units.why: Instructors should align the statement "to your teaching values, beliefs, and course learning objectives", tying AI rules to learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: align to your teaching values, beliefs, and course learning objectives
units.policy: Please modify as you see fit and align to your teaching values, beliefs, and course learning objectives.

units.why: The page offers three named sample statements: "Exploratory Potential", "Permitted Use ... as Specified by the Instructor" and "No Use". Named categories of AI use are P05.
units.anchor: Statement 1: Use of Generative AI as Exploratory Potential
units.policy: The page offers three sample syllabus statements: exploratory use, permitted use as specified by the instructor, and no use of generative AI.

units.why: Sample Statement 1 says "I intend to embed the use of them in my course" and "We will use AI tools for specific activities and assignments", building AI into coursework (P79).
units.anchor: I intend to embed the use of them in my course

units.why: Statement 1 invites students to "share your feedback" while exploring AI together with the instructor, engaging students in discussing the AI approach (P66).
units.anchor: Join me on this exploratory journey and share your feedback
units.fit_note: Invites students to explore AI with the instructor and give feedback, not formally co-create the rules.

units.why: Sample Statement 2 says chatbots "offer valuable benefits if approached responsibly and ethically", a benefit claim, P87.
units.anchor: Generative AI chatbots offer valuable benefits if approached responsibly and ethically

units.why: Statement 2 sends students to "the appropriate sections of this syllabus or individual assignments that reference targeted AI use", so AI permission is set per activity and assignment, P04.
units.anchor: individual assignments that reference targeted AI use
units.policy: For more detailed information, please consult the appropriate sections of this syllabus or individual assignments that reference targeted AI use.

units.why: Statement 2 tells students with questions on whether their use fits to "contact me", the ask-first rule, P10.
units.anchor: If you have questions about how your use of generative AI technologies align
units.policy: If you have questions about how your use of generative AI technologies align with our course and assignment objectives, please contact me so that we may explore together.

units.why: Sample Statement 3 says "The use of generative AI in any form is strictly prohibited in this course", a ban on all AI for the course, P01.
units.anchor: The use of generative AI in any form is strictly prohibited in this course

units.why: Statement 3 bars using AI "to create any content, including ... essays, creative works, code, or solutions for assignments or exams", i.e. AI producing submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: Students are not permitted to employ generative AI tools, algorithms, or models
units.policy: Students are not permitted to employ generative AI tools, algorithms, or models to create any content, including but not limited to essays, creative works, code, or solutions for assignments or exams.

units.why: Statement 3 says chatbot use "will incur the same penalties as plagiarism", classing AI misuse as plagiarism under the Academic Dishonesty process (P36, not P37, since no specific penalty is stated).
units.anchor: Using chatbots in this manner will incur the same penalties as plagiarism

units.why: Statement 3 gives the reason for the ban: "Developing strong competencies in the skills associated with this course ... will prepare you for success", skill-building, P41.
units.anchor: Developing strong competencies in the skills associated with this course
units.policy: Developing strong competencies in the skills associated with this course, from student-based brainstorming to project development, will prepare you for success in your academic and professional journey.

notes: Only the three university-layer documents were coded (school and computing none-found, course deferred). AI-001 is mostly AI governance and procurement, not student coursework; its units are coded as written.
